name: Typescript Conventions
description: This module defines the naming, formatting, and structural style conventions to follow whenever writing, implementing, or reviewing typescript code or output, so results stay consistent with the existing typescript style guide.
content:
This module defines the naming, formatting, and structural style conventions to follow whenever writing, implementing, or reviewing typescript code or output, so results stay consistent with the existing typescript style guide.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Keep typescript outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
2. Re-check edge cases relevant to typescript (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
3. Prefer explicit, readable typescript solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
4. Check that typescript terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
5. Keep typescript changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
6. Measure before optimizing any typescript bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
7. Document any non-obvious typescript decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
8. Surface known limitations of a chosen typescript approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
9. Before starting typescript work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
10. Validate typescript outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
11. When typescript guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not silently drop typescript edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of typescript correctness.
- Do not apply generic typescript advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Do not skip documenting typescript assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Avoid introducing new typescript abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for typescript, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
